Well, it’s... it’s a combination, really, depending on exactly who we're talking about. See, with my family—my mom, my sister—I truly believe they are just mistaken. They don't have the technical background to see what I'm seeing. Like I was saying before, they look at a PDF, they see a date printed at the top in plain text, and they think, 'Okay, well, that's that.' They don't understand that a document can be generated at, say, 10:00 AM, but the metadata might show it was actually compiled and backdated three days later from a completely different secure server. So my family, they aren't lying to me, they're just... they're blinded by their grief, I think, and they just want this whole ordeal to be over. I get that. I really do. It's exhausting for all of us. But I can't just turn off my brain and ignore the actual data. 

Now, the hospital staff and the board members... that is a completely different story. When they sit there in those meetings and explain how the dates and times quote-unquote "match up," they are deliberately relying on the fact that ninety-nine percent of people won't look under the hood. I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and those memorial donation emails all line up perfectly, but when I actually sit down and compare the raw server timestamps, and then factor in the missing attachments—which, by the way, were very clearly stripped out by an automated script before the emails ever hit our inboxes—it paints a completely different picture. 

And you can't just look at the computers, you have to look at the people, too. It's the way certain community members and hospital administrators completely avoid my questions. If I bring up the routing delays, they literally look at the floor, or they suddenly say they have to check with their legal department, or they just physically walk away from me. You don't act like that if it's just a simple clerical error. If it was just a mistake, you'd say, 'Oh, weird, let me check the IT logs.' But they don't. They shut down. So when you put it all together, it’s just incredibly obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. The hospital knows exactly what the data shows, and they're just lying by omission, hoping I'll eventually give up and go away.

Well... see, that’s... that’s a really hypothetical question, Doctor, because you’re asking me to imagine a scenario that fundamentally contradicts the reality of the data I’m looking at every single day. It’s like asking a mathematician, 'If you found out two plus two equaled five, would you accept it?' 

But... okay, if we just play along with this thought experiment... if, somehow, an independent, third-party forensic audit—someone with absolutely zero ties to the hospital board or the local community—came in and proved, beyond a shadow of a doubt, that the server logs were pristine, that the routing delays were just standard packet loss or server latency, and that the missing attachments were never actually there to begin with... I mean, I suppose I would have to accept the technical reality of that. I am a logical person. My whole life is built on logic and empirical evidence. If the data is truly, unequivocally sound, I would have to accept the data.

But... and this is a huge 'but'... even if the digital side of it was somehow completely clean, which, again, I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and donation emails all line up perfectly... even if I accepted that, it wouldn't explain the human element. It just wouldn't. 

Because even if the timestamps were right, why are people acting so strange? Why is it that when I compare the way things are supposed to be handled with how they actually are being handled, there’s this massive disconnect? Even if the missing attachments weren't scrubbed, why won't anyone just look me in the eye and say, 'Here is exactly what happened step-by-step'? Why do certain community members avoid my questions like the plague? 

If it was all just a normal, sad event, people would talk to me. They’d offer condolences and answer my questions, because that’s what people do when there’s nothing to hide. But they don't. They scatter. They get defensive. So, even if you somehow proved the computers were telling the truth, the people aren't. It’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. The technical anomalies are just the breadcrumbs; the way people are behaving is the actual proof that there's a cover-up. So no, I don't think I could just 'accept it' and walk away, because the whole picture—the data and the behavior together—still screams that something is terribly wrong.

Step back... I mean, you ask if I step back. Doctor, I spend half my nights stepping back and trying to look at this from every conceivable angle. In my line of work, we call it stress-testing the system. You try to break your own model to see if it holds up. But every single time I do that, the model breaks. When I actually sit there and compare the exact discrepancies in the timestamps, and I look at the digital footprint of those missing attachments... and then I combine that with the physical, real-world reality of the situation. The way certain community members, people who have known my family for years, completely avoid my questions now. They won't even look me in the eye, or they literally cross the street when they see me coming. 

You don't get that specific, coordinated combination of digital scrubbing and human evasion by accident. It just doesn't happen in a vacuum. So to answer your question... no, I don't really wonder if my interpretation is incorrect anymore. I've done the math. I've run the variables over and over. It’s overwhelmingly obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. I wouldn't be putting myself through this, I wouldn't be sitting here right now letting my own mother and sister think I'm losing my grip, if I wasn't absolutely, unequivocally certain.

Well, if we’re looking at an exact timeline... I mean, the initial shock of his passing was one thing, you know? You wipe the event viewer. That is Sysadmin 101 for covering your tracks. So, frankly, if this expert found literally no trace of the command, it wouldn't prove the file was never deleted.
